doctoral research

Making life coherent

An ethnography in plant biotechnology laboratories in Chile

The research follows the practices through which the Chilean biotechnological ecosystem transforms living organisms into materials, data and promises for the future. Its focus is not only on what happens inside the laboratory, but also on the relationships that connect scientific research, gene banks, public institutions, companies and environmental problems.

The problem

Life does not arrive at the laboratory as a ready-made object

To be known and intervened, plant life must be extracted from its contexts, fragmented and translated into samples, sequences, databases and other forms of information. These operations allow organisms to be compared, circulate between spaces and project new interventions, but they also produce losses, frictions and imbalances.

Biotechnology thus works with entities that are never completely stable or controllable. Producing knowledge requires coordinating materials, techniques, biological rhythms, experiments, institutions and future expectations. The thesis examines how these coordinations acquire consistency and what happens when they are interrupted or overwhelmed.

Research question

What happens to plant life when it is translated into genetic information and how do the material, temporal and institutional operations that make this translation possible produce and stress its coherence as a scientific object?

Core concept

Coherence without homogeneity

In this research, coherence does not mean that differences disappear or that all parts form a stable unit. It designates a practical and provisional effect through which organisms, data, techniques and institutions can operate as if they refer to the same object, although their materialities, histories and temporalities continue to be different.

Asking about coherence allows us to observe both the work that sustains these articulations and the tensions that make them partial, fragile and reviewable.

Three analytical axes

Operations that make a scientific object possible

01

From matter to information

I follow the transformations through which plants, tissues and samples become comparable sequences, records and data. I am interested in what is preserved, what is lost and what new possibilities of intervention appear during that translation.

02

Temporalities that do not quite align

Growth rates, experimental times, funding cycles, and institutional urgencies must be coordinated, although they never completely coincide. Consistency depends on temporary fixes that can fail, delay, or be overwhelmed.

03

Future promises

Drought, productivity, innovation and climate adaptation are not just external contexts: they organize scientific priorities, investments and ways of imagining what plant lives should be known, conserved or transformed.

Ethnographic approach

Pursue relationships beyond a single lab

The research adopts a multi-sited approach that follows materials, documents, techniques and people through different spaces of the Chilean biotechnological ecosystem:

  • plant biotechnology laboratories;
  • germplasm banks and collections;
  • state institutions and programs;
  • companies and associations linked to biotechnology.

The work combines participant observation, interviews, monitoring of experimental processes and document analysis. Rather than assuming in advance where the object begins or ends, ethnography accompanies the operations that make it circulate and change shape.

Complementary horizon

Material experimentation

The doctoral thesis is developed through ethnography and its central result will be written. In parallel, projects such as Viejito-Perro or the Huerto explore the construction of sensors, domestic infrastructures and forms of representation as complementary ways of thinking with environments, organisms and data.

These explorations function as a horizon of material experimentation from which to test other relationships between observation, intervention and knowledge.
